medium.q: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard pack of 52. What is the probability that both are aces?
In how many ways can 7 people sit around a circular table?

hard.q: How many non-negative integer solutions does x + y + z = 12 have?

hard.q: There are 10 points in a plane, of which 4 lie on one straight line and no other three are collinear. How many triangles can be formed?
hard.why: Subtract the collinear triples from all triples.

hard.q: In how many ways can the letters of the word DAUGHTER be arranged so that no two vowels are next to each other?
hard.why: Place consonants first, then put the vowels in the gaps between them.

hard.q: Two fair dice are rolled and at least one shows a 5. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
hard.why: Conditional probability: restrict to the 11 outcomes with a 5.

easy.q:
When a delivery app raises its fees during a downpour, customers grumble and call it profiteering. Economists tend to see something else. A higher price does two jobs at once: it nudges some customers to wait for the rain to stop, and it tempts more riders to leave their homes and take orders. Without the price rise, demand would stay high while the supply of riders shrank, and the app would simply run out of people to deliver, leaving everyone worse off. Critics reply that this logic assumes riders are free agents who can choose when to work. Many depend on a daily target to repay a motorbike loan, and for them a rainy night is not a chance to earn more but a pressure to ride in unsafe conditions. The price signal may work on the screen, then, while quietly transferring the risk to those least able to bear it.

Question: According to the passage, what two jobs does a higher delivery fee do during rain?
o: It discourages some customers from ordering and attracts more riders to work
It raises the app's profit and punishes careless customers
It cuts the number of riders and raises demand
It lets riders repay loans and lets customers order faster
easy.why: The passage says the price nudges customers to wait and tempts more riders to take orders.

easy.q:
For decades the neighbourhood kirana survived because it sold something no supermarket could: credit and familiarity. The shopkeeper knew which families ran short before the month's end and let the ledger run. Quick-commerce start-ups arrived with a different promise, groceries in ten minutes, funded by investors willing to lose money on each order in exchange for customer habit. Early on, kirana owners lost many evening orders. But a pattern has since emerged in several cities. Households use the apps for forgotten items and impulse purchases, while the weekly stock-up of rice, oil and pulses still flows to the corner shop, often on credit. The apps, it turns out, compete with the kirana for convenience, not for trust. Whether investors will keep paying for convenience alone will decide how long this arrangement lasts. If the subsidies end and delivery fees rise, the apps' advantage in speed may no longer justify the price.

Question: According to the passage, what did the kirana offer that supermarkets could not?
easy.why: The first sentence names credit and familiarity.

easy.q:
When the price of a packet of biscuits rises from ₹10 to ₹12, shoppers notice at once. When it stays at ₹10 but the packet quietly shrinks from 80 grams to 68, most do not. Companies have long understood this asymmetry. A higher sticker price invites comparison with rivals, while a lighter pack is noticed only by those who check the small print on the wrapper. Economists call the practice shrinkflation, and statisticians worry about it more than shoppers do. Consumer price indices track the prices of items, and if the items are not adjusted for size, measured inflation understates the real rise in cost. Some agencies now adjust for pack size, but the exercise is laborious and possible only where weights are printed. Defenders of the firms argue that the costs of wheat, palm oil and packaging rise whatever they do, and that shrinking the pack is gentler on buyers with tight budgets than a sudden price jump. That defence, however, concedes the main point: the buyer is paying more per gram.

Question: According to the passage, shrinkflation is the practice of
o: reducing a pack's size while keeping its price the same
raising prices on small packs only
easy.why: The biscuit example shows the price staying at ₹10 while the weight falls.

When the price of a packet of biscuits rises from ₹10 to ₹12, shoppers notice at once. When it stays at ₹10 but the packet quietly shrinks from 80 grams to 68, most do not. Along the Sundarbans coast, villagers say that the forest took the cyclone's first blow so that the village did not have to. The claim has a physical basis. Mangrove roots form a dense tangle that slows incoming water, and a belt a few hundred metres wide can reduce wave height considerably before it reaches an embankment. Recent studies suggest that a healthy belt is often cheaper per kilometre protected than a seawall of similar effect, and it repairs itself after storms instead of needing a budget line. The catch is that the benefit depends on the forest being dense and wide, and aquaculture ponds, firewood cutting and rising salinity have thinned it in many places. A thinned belt may look green from the road yet offer far less protection than its appearance suggests.

easy.q:
Training a large language model consumes electricity on a scale that surprises people who think of software as weightless. A single training run can draw as much power as thousands of homes use over weeks, and the cooling of data centres adds a further demand for water. Yet focusing on training alone gives a misleading picture. Once a model is released, it is queried millions of times a day, and the total energy spent answering those queries can, over a model's lifetime, exceed the energy spent creating it. Researchers have shown that smaller models, trained on carefully chosen data, can match larger ones on narrow tasks at a fraction of the cost. The difficulty is that the industry rewards headline size: bigger models attract more attention and investment. Unless efficiency is measured and reported as routinely as accuracy, the incentive to shrink will remain weaker than the incentive to scale.

o: A demand for new training data
easy.why: Cooling is said to add a further demand for water.

easy.q:
Sleep is not merely rest for the brain; it appears to be a workshop. During the deep stages of sleep, patterns of neural activity recorded during the day are replayed, often faster than they first occurred. Researchers believe this replay helps convert fragile new memories into stable ones, which is why a student who sleeps after studying often recalls more than one who stays awake revising. The picture is not a simple one, however. Sleep seems to favour the memories that are linked to a future goal, such as an exam, over those that are incidental. It also does not store everything: experiments suggest that some weak connections are deliberately dimmed overnight, perhaps to keep the brain from saturating. If so, forgetting is not a failure of the system but one of its working parts. This complicates the popular advice to 'sleep on it', which assumes sleep merely preserves whatever we put in.

o: Patterns recorded during the day are replayed, often faster

easy.why: The first lines describe replay of daytime patterns.

easy.q:
Two drivers leave a party after the same number of drinks and take the same road. One reaches home; the other hits a child who runs into the street. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly, though both made an identical choice. Philosophers call this puzzle moral luck: the idea that we are judged partly by outcomes beyond our control. The usual response is to insist that blame should track only what the person chose and knew. Yet our everyday practice resists this. We feel that the driver who caused a death has something to answer for that the lucky driver lacks, and the driver himself often feels it more than anyone. One might say this feeling is an error that careful reflection should remove. Another view holds that it reveals something true: that we are agents who act in a world, not only minds who intend, and that responsibility cannot be cleanly separated from what our actions actually do.

Question: The two drivers in the opening example are used to show that
o: the same choice can be judged very differently depending on the outcome
only the second driver was drunk
easy.why: Both made an identical choice, yet outcomes shaped the judgement.

easy.q:
Psychologists have long observed that once people learn how an event turned out, they tend to believe they predicted it. This hindsight bias makes the past seem more orderly than it was, and it is difficult to remove: warning subjects about it barely reduces it. One explanation is that the mind does not store old beliefs and new facts in separate boxes. When the outcome is learned, memory is quietly reconstructed around it, so that earlier doubts fade and the final result seems to have been visible all along. The bias has costs beyond embarrassment. Investigators of accidents, for example, find it hard to be fair to the people involved, because the warning signs that look obvious now were buried among many harmless signals at the time. A better practice, some argue, is to reconstruct what the person actually knew at each moment, rather than to ask why they failed to see what we now see.

Question: Hindsight bias is the tendency to
o: believe, once an outcome is known, that one predicted it
forget all events that went well
easy.why: It is defined at the start of the passage.

easy.q:
The ship of Theseus is a puzzle about identity. If every plank of a wooden ship is gradually replaced, is it still the same ship? Most people say yes, since the ship has kept its form and its history. But suppose someone collects the discarded planks and rebuilds the old ship. Now two ships stand in the harbour, and each has a claim to be the original. The puzzle matters because people undergo similar replacement: nearly every cell in the body is renewed over years, and memories and beliefs change. If sameness required the same material, none of us would be the same person who began school. Some philosophers conclude that identity is a matter of continuity, an unbroken chain of small changes, not of unchanging parts. The rebuilt ship then fails the test, because there is no continuous chain between its planks and the voyages the ship made. Others think this answer simply settles a question that remains open.

Question: The ship of Theseus puzzle asks whether
o: a ship can sail without planks
a ship remains the same when all its planks are replaced
easy.why: It is stated in the second sentence.

The stepwells of western India were never only reservoirs. In the dry months, a woman descending the steps to fetch water entered a cool, shaded room where neighbours met, news travelled and travellers rested. The carvings that line the walls, of goddesses, musicians and everyday scenes, suggest that builders thought of the structure as a public building as much as a utility. Historians note that many were commissioned by women of the royal household, which is one of the few areas of monumental building where women's patronage is well recorded. With piped water, the wells fell out of use, and colonial surveyors often described them as curiosities. What was lost was not merely a source of water. When a community stops gathering at the same place for a necessary chore, it loses the casual encounters that held it together, and no tap, however reliable, replaces them.

easy.why: The passage says many were commissioned by women of the royal household.

Written records are often treated as the surest evidence of the past, but the preference is more habit than logic. Documents were produced by those who could write, usually officials and merchants, and they recorded what such people thought worth keeping: taxes, land grants, disputes. The lives of herders, potters and weavers appear mostly as items in someone else's account. Oral traditions, by contrast, were kept by the people they described, and the ballads of many regions preserve events that no register mentions. They are not, of course, free from distortion; a singer may flatter a patron or compress centuries into a single hero. But documents flatter patrons too. The historian's task, then, is not to rank the two kinds of source but to ask of each who made it, for whom, and what it would have been convenient to leave out. A fact supported by both is stronger than a fact in either alone.

Before the railways, towns in India kept their own time, set by the sun at noon, and a few minutes' difference between two cities troubled nobody. A traveller on a bullock cart crossed a region so slowly that the gap did not matter. The timetable changed this. A train that left at a fixed hour could not wait for local noon, and the railway companies adopted a single standard for their operations. Over the following decades, offices, courts and schools followed, since it was impractical to run a day by two clocks. Some historians argue that the new discipline of the clock served the colonial economy by making labour measurable and predictable. Others point out that Indians also used it for their own purposes, to run trams, newspapers and political meetings. The truth may be that a technology introduced for one end proved useful for many, which is not the same as being neutral.

easy.why: Each town kept its own time set by local noon.

The truth may be that a technology introduced for one end proved useful for many, which is not the same as being neutral.

Question: 'Which is not the same as being neutral' most nearly means that
o: the technology was used by no one
a technology that serves many ends may still carry the discipline of its original purpose
hard.why: Being useful for many ends does not show it is free of the original design's bias.

hard.q:
Before the railways, towns in India kept their own time, set by the sun at noon, and a few minutes' difference between two cities troubled nobody. A traveller on a bullock cart crossed a region so slowly that the gap did not matter. The timetable changed this. A train that left at a fixed hour could not wait for local noon, and the railway companies adopted a single standard for their operations. Over the following decades, offices, courts and schools followed, since it was impractical to run a day by two clocks. Some historians argue that the new discipline of the clock served the colonial economy by making labour measurable and predictable. Others point out that Indians also used it for their own purposes, to run trams, newspapers and political meetings. The truth may be that a technology introduced for one end proved useful for many, which is not the same as being neutral.

Question: Which finding would most weaken the historians who think the clock mainly served the colonial economy?
o: Railways were built by the colonial state
Indian-owned factories adopted fixed hours before colonial offices did, for their own reasons
hard.why: If Indian enterprises adopted it first for their own ends, the 'colonial' reading weakens.

easy.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. She waited till the water boiled, then added tea leaves and a little ginger.
B. Meera filled a kettle with water and set it on the stove.
C. Finally she strained the tea into two cups and called her father.
D. She let it simmer for two minutes until the colour deepened.

Question: Which is the correct order?
easy.why: The steps run in time order: fill the kettle, boil and add leaves, simmer, then strain and serve.

easy.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. It was built in 1911 and has carried trains ever since.
B. The old railway bridge over the Mahi river will close for repairs next month.
C. Engineers found that its iron girders have rusted badly.
D. Until it reopens, trains will take a longer route via Anand.

Question: Which is the correct order?
easy.why: B introduces the bridge. A ('It was built') and C ('its iron girders') refer back to it. D ('Until it reopens') closes the paragraph.

medium.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. Chai sellers, however, kept the price-sensitive customers who pass their stalls every morning.
B. Coffee chains entered Indian metros in the late 1990s, promising a premium experience.
C. Their survival shows that a new habit does not always replace an old one; it can sit beside it.
D. Within a decade, a café meeting had become a normal part of a young professional's week.

Question: Which is the correct order?
medium.why: B opens with the chains. D follows ('Within a decade'). A needs the contrast signalled by 'however', and C ('Their survival') needs A's chai sellers before it.

medium.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. Pricing seats cheaply to fill planes brought flying within reach of first-time travellers.
B. Low-cost airlines in India dropped meals and free baggage to cut costs.
C. Airports soon struggled with crowds they had not been built for.
D. Demand for domestic flights grew faster than anyone had planned for.

Question: Which is the correct order?
medium.why: Cause runs to effect: cost cutting (B), cheap seats (A), demand growth (D), crowded airports (C).

hard.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. Yet that habit of checking has a cost, since time spent verifying is time not spent doing the work.
B. Where institutions are trusted, people can hand over a task without inspecting how it is done.
C. Where they are not, every transaction needs a witness, a receipt or a second opinion.
D. Economists sometimes describe trust as a way of saving effort rather than as a feeling.

Question: Which is the correct order?
hard.why: D states the idea and is the only sentence that works as an opener. B and C then contrast trusting and distrusting settings, and A ('that habit of checking', 'Yet') refers back to C.

hard.q:
The four sentences below are jumbled. Choose the order that makes the most logical paragraph.

A. The finding unsettled researchers who had assumed that more screen time simply meant less sleep.
B. In a study of 2,000 teenagers, those who read on a tablet before bed slept no worse than those who read printed books.
C. What mattered, it turned out, was whether the content was calming or exciting.
D. Screen brightness, by contrast, made almost no measurable difference.

Question: Which is the correct order?
hard.why: B reports the study. A ('The finding') reacts to it. C gives what did matter, and D ('by contrast') contrasts brightness with that content effect.

easy.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

Stepwells in Gujarat were never just places to draw water. Travellers rested in their cool chambers, women met there to talk, and festivals were held at the water's edge. When piped water arrived, most stepwells were abandoned, and today they survive mostly as tourist sights.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Stepwells in Gujarat are now popular tourist sights.
Piped water has damaged India's heritage.
Stepwells served as social spaces as well as water sources, and lost their role once piped water arrived.
Travellers preferred stepwells to inns when they journeyed.
easy.why: The passage gives stepwells two roles, water and community life, and says the second faded with piped water. The other options take one detail or add a claim.

easy.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

When a Pune school let children grow vegetables, attendance rose and lunch waste fell. Pupils who had refused to eat greens began to taste what they had planted. Teachers also noticed that the garden gave quiet children a chance to lead.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Vegetables grown at school are tastier than market vegetables.
Quiet children should be given leadership roles in every school.
Schools in Pune have higher attendance than other schools.
A school garden changed children's eating habits and confidence, and not just their knowledge of plants.
easy.why: The passage lists better attendance, less waste, more eating of greens and a leadership chance. The correct option covers these effects without extra claims.

medium.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

Rating systems promise fairness: a customer scores a driver, and the score decides who gets work. But a score squeezes a messy trip into a single number, and it is rarely clear what caused a low one: a late train, a rude passenger, a wrong turn on the map. Workers learn to chase the number rather than the service, thanking customers for five stars and avoiding difficult routes. The system measures behaviour, then quietly reshapes it.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Ratings that look fair reduce complex service to a number, and workers end up serving the number.
Drivers have learned to thank passengers for five stars.
Customers should stop rating the people who serve them.
Technology has made work worse for most people.
medium.why: The core claim is that a single score misreads and then reshapes behaviour. Thanking customers is only one example, and the other options go beyond the passage.

medium.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

Monsoon forecasts have improved sharply: models now track rain-bearing systems days ahead. Yet a farmer rarely acts on a forecast for a whole district. What matters is whether rain will reach the village before the sowing window closes. Until forecasts are issued at that scale, better science will not become better harvests.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Science alone cannot solve the problems of Indian agriculture.
Better monsoon forecasts will help farmers only when they are specific to the village and the sowing window.
Monsoon models can now track rain systems several days ahead.
Farmers should ignore district-level forecasts altogether.
medium.why: The claim is conditional and specific: scale decides whether forecasts help. 'Science alone' is too broad and the tracking detail is too narrow.

hard.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

Nostalgia is usually dismissed as a longing for a past that never was, a sentimental editing of memory. But research suggests the dismissal is hasty. People who recall warm moments report feeling more connected and more willing to help strangers, which suggests nostalgia works less as an escape from the present than as a resource for it. The risk lies elsewhere: when whole societies borrow the feeling to promise a return, a private comfort becomes a political tool.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Nostalgia is harmful because it distorts memory and escapes reality.
Nostalgia makes people more willing to help strangers.
Nostalgia, often waved away as sentimental, can strengthen connection in the present, though collectively invoked it can become a political instrument.
Societies should never promise a return to the past.
hard.why: The passage defends nostalgia, then warns about its collective use. Option two keeps only the first half and the others reverse the tone or overstate it.

hard.q:
Read the passage and pick the option that best summarises it.

Cities that widen roads to ease traffic often find the congestion returns within a few years. The new lanes make driving quicker and so attract trips that people had earlier postponed, shared or given up. Planners therefore treat road space as something that generates its own demand, and some now measure success not by speed but by how many people a street moves.

Question: Which option is the best summary of the passage?
o: Congestion returns within a few years of widening a road.
Cities should stop building roads and ban private cars.
Road widening is too expensive for most cities.
Added road capacity brings new trips, so congestion returns, and some planners now judge streets by people moved, not vehicle speed.
hard.why: The passage links widening to induced demand and then to a changed measure of success. The wrong options give only the first step, an unsupported cost claim, or an extreme policy.

easy.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. Kaju katli is made by grinding cashews and cooking them with sugar syrup.
2. The warm mixture is rolled flat and cut into diamonds.
3. A thin sheet of edible silver is laid on top before packing.
4. Many families buy a box from the same sweet shop every Diwali.
5. The pieces are cooled completely before they are boxed.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
easy.why: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 describe how the sweet is made. Sentence 4 is about buying habits.

easy.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. Mumbai's local trains slow down when tracks flood.
2. Roads at low-lying junctions fill with water within an hour of heavy rain.
3. Schools often declare a holiday after a red alert.
4. Delhi's winter mornings are often covered by dense fog.
5. Civic workers pump water out of underpasses to keep traffic moving.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
easy.why: All other sentences describe the monsoon's effects on Mumbai. Sentence 4 is about winter fog in Delhi.

medium.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. Since 2020 the town library has lent e-books to members at home.
2. Its reading rooms now stay open until 10 pm for students preparing for exams.
3. A children's corner opened last year and fills up with families on weekends.
4. The building was designed by a British engineer and finished in 1910.
5. It has also started free weekend classes in spoken English.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
medium.why: The theme is how the library has adapted to its readers. Sentence 4 is about the building's design and date.

medium.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. Uniforms reduce visible differences of wealth in a classroom.
2. They also spare parents a daily argument over what to wear.
3. Critics reply that sameness can suppress a child's sense of self.
4. Honestly, nothing says 'learning' like a tie that chokes you in May.
5. The evidence on results is mixed, so the argument rests more on values than on data.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
medium.why: The other sentences weigh the uniform debate in a measured way. Sentence 4 is a flippant joke.

hard.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. UPI grew quickly because any bank account holder could pay with just a phone number.
2. Small shopkeepers adopted it because it cost them nothing, unlike card machines.
3. Its open design let many apps compete on the same rails.
4. Mobile data prices fell sharply in the mid-2010s, which made phone payments affordable.
5. Surveys show that some older rural customers still fear scams, which keeps them tied to cash.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
hard.why: Sentences 1 to 4 give reasons for UPI's rapid growth. Sentence 5 describes a limit on adoption.

hard.q:
Five sentences on a theme are given below; four belong together and one does not.

1. Prices of staple goods rise by a few per cent every year.
2. Over decades, this makes fixed savings buy much less.
3. Savers therefore look for returns above the rate of inflation.
4. The RBI targets retail inflation at 4 per cent, with a tolerance band of 2 points either side.
5. A fixed deposit that pays less than inflation loses value in real terms.

Question: Which sentence does not belong?
hard.why: The paragraph is about what inflation does to savers. Sentence 4 turns to the central bank's policy target.

easy.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Bengaluru's lakes were once linked by channels that carried water from one lake to the next.
2. As the city grew, many of these channels were built over.
3. Heavy rain now floods streets that were once drained safely.
4. Restoring even a few channels would help.

Sentence to place: "Without these links, rainwater has nowhere to go."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
easy.why: 'These links' refers to the channels that were built over in sentence 2, and the sentence explains the flooding in sentence 3.

easy.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Many people think a savings account is the safest place for all their money.
2. It is safe, and the money can be withdrawn at any time.
3. The interest rate, however, is often lower than the rise in prices.
4. That is why experts suggest keeping only an emergency fund there.

Sentence to place: "Over a few years, this slowly shrinks what the money can buy."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
easy.why: 'This' refers to interest lagging behind price rises in sentence 3, and the new sentence leads to the advice in sentence 4.

medium.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Ravi's bakery was close to shutting down in 2019.
2. He had borrowed money to buy a second oven, but sales did not rise.
3. So he began delivering through an app and cut his menu to six items.
4. By 2022 he was repaying the loan early.

Sentence to place: "The extra oven stood idle for most of the day."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
medium.why: 'The extra oven' needs the second oven introduced in sentence 2, and the sentence explains why sales did not rise, which leads to the 'So' of sentence 3.

medium.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Many believe that a good memory is a gift of birth.
2. Studies of London taxi drivers show something different.
3. And the longer they had been on the road, the larger that area was.
4. The brain, in other words, behaves more like a muscle than like a fixed possession.

Sentence to place: "The area of the brain linked to navigation was larger in drivers who had passed the city's hard test than in ordinary adults."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
medium.why: The sentence needs taxi drivers to be introduced first, and sentence 3 ('that area was larger') depends on the sentence naming the brain area.

hard.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Public libraries in the nineteenth century were often founded by factory owners.
2. Their motive was not pure generosity.
3. A literate worker could follow safety rules and run new machines.
4. Yet the habit of reading, once started, could not be steered.

Sentence to place: "Books, they hoped, would also keep workers away from taverns and union meetings."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
hard.why: 'Also' adds a second hope after the benefit in sentence 3, and 'Yet' in sentence 4 contradicts the idea that reading could be steered.

hard.q:
A paragraph has four numbered sentences, and one sentence has been removed from it.

1. Languages rarely die because people stop loving them.
2. They die when the daily reasons to use them disappear.
3. A child who needs another language to study, earn or even joke with friends gradually stops answering in the home tongue.
4. By the time the grandparents notice, the chain of speakers has broken.

Sentence to place: "Affection, in short, is not enough to keep a language alive."

Question: After which numbered sentence does it fit best?
hard.why: 'In short' sums up the argument, which is complete only after sentence 4. Earlier positions would cut off the example and its consequence.

easy.q: Which word is a collective noun?
easy.why: A herd is a group of animals taken as one.

easy.q: What is the plural of 'child'?
easy.why: Child has an irregular plural.

easy.q: In 'Her honesty impressed the teacher', which word is an abstract noun?
easy.why: Honesty is a quality you cannot touch.

easy.q: Meera is my best friend. ___ lives near my house. Choose the pronoun.
easy.why: Meera is one girl, so we use 'She'.

easy.q: What is the plural of 'knife'?
easy.why: Nouns ending in -fe change to -ves.

easy.q: Replace the noun in 'The boys played cricket' with a pronoun.
easy.why: 'The boys' is plural and third person, so 'They'.

medium.q: Which sentence has a collective noun?
o: A swarm of bees settled on the tree.
medium.why: Swarm names a group of bees.

medium.q: Which pair is correctly matched as singular and plural?
medium.why: Mouse and goose are irregular; wolf makes wolves; sheep stays sheep.

medium.q: Which is the abstract noun in 'The villagers admired Anil's courage during the flood'?
medium.why: Courage is a quality; the others are things or people.

medium.q: Ravi and I went to the market. ___ bought mangoes. Choose the pronoun.
medium.why: 'Ravi and I' is the subject, so we use 'We'.

medium.q: What are the plurals of 'baby' and 'monkey'?
medium.why: Consonant + y becomes -ies; vowel + y just adds -s.

medium.q: The teacher gave the prize to Neha and ___. Choose the correct word.
medium.why: After 'to' we need the object form 'me'.

hard.q: In 'Kabir showed kindness to the dog', the nouns Kabir, kindness and dog are respectively:
hard.why: Kabir names a person, kindness is a quality, dog is a general name.

hard.q: Which sentence has all the plurals correct?
o: The two mans carried three boxes of tomatoes.
The two men carried three boxs of tomatoes.
The two men carried three boxes of tomatoes.
The two mens carried three boxes of tomatos.
hard.why: Man becomes men; box takes -es; tomato takes -es.

hard.q: Which noun is used only in the plural form?
hard.why: Scissors is always plural in form.

hard.q: The little boy hurt ___ while climbing the wall. Choose the pronoun.
hard.why: A reflexive pronoun must match the boy: himself.

hard.q: Which noun has the same form in singular and plural?
hard.why: Deer is both one deer and many deer.

hard.q: Which sentence uses the possessive pronoun correctly?
o: This pen is my, not your.
This pen is mine, not yours.
This pen is me, not you.
This pen is mine, not your.
hard.why: Mine and yours stand alone without a noun after them.

easy.q: Choose the article: ___ apple a day keeps the doctor away.
easy.why: Apple starts with a vowel sound, so 'an'.

easy.q: Fill in: I have ___ pencils in my box. (a small number, countable)
easy.why: Few is used with countable plural nouns.

easy.q: Choose the article: She bought ___ umbrella.
easy.why: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound /u/ as in 'up'.

easy.q: Choose the demonstrative: ___ book here on my desk is new.
easy.why: 'Here' and one book mean 'This'.

easy.q: Fill in: There is ___ milk in the glass. (not full)
easy.why: Some fits an uncountable noun like milk.

easy.q: Choose the word: Aman lost ___ bag yesterday.
easy.why: 'His' is the possessive that goes before a noun.

medium.q: Choose the article: He is ___ honest boy.
medium.why: Honest starts with a vowel sound because h is silent.

medium.q: Which sentence is correct?
medium.why: Water is uncountable, so 'a little'.

medium.q: Choose the article: Ravi is ___ European student.
medium.why: European begins with a 'y' sound, a consonant sound.

medium.q: Fill in: ___ birds over there are sparrows.
medium.why: Far and plural means 'Those'.

medium.q: Which sentence is correct?
medium.why: Mangoes are countable, so 'many'.

medium.q: Fill in: The girls forgot ___ lunch boxes.
medium.why: 'Their' shows the girls own the boxes.

hard.q: Which sentence needs 'the' in the blank? ___ Ganga is a holy river.
hard.why: Names of rivers take 'the'.

hard.q: Which sentence uses 'little' correctly to mean 'almost none'?
o: There is little hope of rain today.
There is a little hope of rain today.
There are little hopes of rain.
There is few hope of rain today.
hard.why: 'Little' without 'a' is negative: hardly any.

hard.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The sun rises in a east.
The sun rises in the east.
hard.why: Unique things like the sun take 'the', and 'the east' too.

hard.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Two those red balls are mine.
Red two those balls are mine.
Those two red balls are mine.
Those red two ball are mine.
hard.why: Determiners such as 'those' come before numbers and adjectives.

hard.q: Which sentence uses 'few' to mean 'some, enough'?
o: Few guests arrived early, so we had help.
A few guests arrived early, so we started.
hard.why: 'A few' is positive: some.

hard.q: Which sentence has the article error?
hard.why: University starts with a 'yoo' sound so 'a' is needed.

easy.q: Choose the correct verb: She ___ to school every day.
easy.why: Third person singular takes -es in simple present.

easy.q: Choose the correct form: Birds ___ in the sky now.
easy.why: Plural subject and 'now' need 'are flying'.

easy.q: Choose the past form: Yesterday, we ___ to the park.
easy.why: Go has an irregular past: went.

easy.q: Choose the correct form: Tomorrow I ___ my grandmother.
easy.why: Tomorrow shows future, so 'will visit'.

easy.q: Choose the correct form: He ___ his homework right now.
easy.why: 'Right now' needs present continuous with 'is'.

easy.q: Which sentence is in the future tense?
easy.why: 'Will play' marks the future.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: My father ___ tea every morning.
medium.why: Habit in the present; he takes -s.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: The children ___ when the teacher came in.
medium.why: Past continuous with plural subject: were talking.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: She ___ her room yesterday.
medium.why: Yesterday needs simple past.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: Next week, Priya ___ to Jaipur.
medium.why: 'Next week' shows the future.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: I ___ a letter when the lights went out.
medium.why: An action in progress in the past uses 'was writing'.

medium.q: Choose the correct form: Do you know if it ___ tomorrow?
medium.why: A future event needs 'will rain'.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: He did not go to school yesterday.
He did not went to school yesterday.
He not went to school yesterday.
He did not goes to school yesterday.
hard.why: After 'did not' use the base verb: go.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I was read while my sister cooked.
I read while my sister was cook.
I was reading while my sister was cooking.
I am reading while my sister was cooking.
hard.why: Two actions going on together in the past use past continuous.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
hard.why: After 'does' use the base verb: play.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The sun rises in the east.
The sun rose in the east every day.
The sun is rise in the east.
The sun rising in the east.
hard.why: General truths use the simple present.

hard.q: Which sentence has the verb tense error?
o: Yesterday I went to the market.
Tomorrow I will go to the market.
Now I am going to the market.
Yesterday I will go to the market.
hard.why: 'Yesterday' cannot be used with 'will go'.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay home.
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
If it rained tomorrow, we stay home.
If it rains tomorrow, we stayed home.
hard.why: After 'if' we use present, not 'will', for a future condition.

easy.q: Choose the preposition: The cat is sleeping ___ the table.
easy.why: Under shows place; the others are not prepositions of place.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: Mohan was born ___ 2014.
easy.why: Use 'in' with years.

easy.q: Choose the preposition: School starts ___ 8 o'clock.
easy.why: Use 'at' with a clock time.

easy.q: Choose the conjunction: I like tea ___ coffee.
easy.why: 'And' joins two similar things.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: We play cricket ___ Sundays.
easy.why: Use 'on' with days.

easy.q: Choose the conjunction: She was tired, ___ she kept walking.
easy.why: 'But' shows contrast.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: The bird flew ___ the window.
medium.why: Through shows movement from one side to the other.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: I am afraid ___ dogs.
medium.why: 'Afraid of' is the right phrase.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: She is good ___ painting.
medium.why: 'Good at' is the fixed phrase.

medium.q: Choose the conjunction: Hurry up, ___ you will miss the bus.
medium.why: 'Or' warns of what happens otherwise.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: He is interested ___ music.
medium.why: 'Interested in' is correct.

medium.q: Choose the conjunction: He stayed home ___ he was ill.
medium.why: 'Because' gives the reason.

hard.q: Choose the correct word: The books were divided ___ the three girls.
hard.why: Use 'among' for more than two.

hard.q: Choose the correct word: He has lived here ___ 2019.
hard.why: 'Since' goes with a starting point in time.

hard.q: Choose the correct word: The ball rolled ___ the two chairs.
hard.why: Between is used for two.

hard.q: Choose the conjunction: ___ it was raining, we went out to play.
hard.why: Although shows the surprising contrast.

hard.q: Choose the correct word: She has been waiting ___ two hours.
hard.why: 'For' goes with a length of time.

hard.q: Choose the conjunction: You cannot enter ___ you show your ticket.
hard.why: 'Unless' means 'if not'.

easy.q: Which word is an adjective in 'The red kite flew high'?
easy.why: Red describes the kite.

easy.q: Choose the adverb: She sings sweetly.
easy.why: Sweetly tells how she sings.

easy.q: Choose the comparative: Ria is ___ than Sia. (tall)
easy.why: Add -er to short adjectives to compare two.

easy.q: Choose the superlative: Mount Everest is the ___ mountain. (high)
easy.why: The superlative of high is highest.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: He runs ___. (quick)
easy.why: A verb is described by an adverb.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: This box is ___ than that one. (heavy)
easy.why: Change y to i and add -er.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: Of all the boys, Dev is the ___. (good)
medium.why: Good - better - best is irregular.

medium.q: Which word is an adverb of time? 'We will leave soon.'
medium.why: Soon tells when.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: This story is ___ than that one. (interesting)
medium.why: Long adjectives take 'more'.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: She answered the question ___. (correct)
medium.why: An adverb describes how she answered.

medium.q: Which word is an adverb of place? 'The children played outside.'
medium.why: Outside tells where.

medium.q: Choose the correct word: She is the ___ girl in the class. (young)
medium.why: Three or more things need superlative.

hard.q: Choose the correct word: He is ___ than his brother. (clever)
hard.why: Two persons: comparative; clever takes -er.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: He did good in the test.
He did goodly in the test.
He did well in the test.
He did best in the test, than me.
hard.why: 'Well' is the adverb; 'good' is an adjective.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She is the beautifulest girl here.
She is the most beautiful girl here.
She is more beautiful girl here.
hard.why: Long adjectives take most for the superlative.

hard.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: This is the less expensive of the two bags.
This is the least expensive of the two bags.
This is the less expensive from the two bags.
hard.why: With two, we use the comparative: less.

hard.q: Which sentence has an adverb modifying an adjective?
hard.why: 'Very' describes the adjective 'hot'.

hard.q: Choose the correct sentence.
hard.why: 'Late' is the adverb meaning not on time; 'lately' means recently.

easy.q: In 'my sister lives in jaipur.' which word needs a capital letter?
easy.why: Names of places are proper nouns and begin with a capital.

easy.q: Which sentence is an exclamatory sentence?
easy.why: It shows sudden strong feeling.

easy.q: Which sentence needs a question mark?
easy.why: It is a question.

easy.q: Choose the correct sentence.
easy.why: Apostrophe replaces the o in 'do not'.

easy.q: Which is a command?
easy.why: A command tells someone to do something.

easy.q: Which sentence has a comma used correctly?
o: I bought, apples bananas and grapes.
I bought apples bananas, and, grapes.
I, bought apples bananas and grapes.
I bought apples, bananas and grapes.
easy.why: Commas separate items in a list.

medium.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
medium.why: Comma comes after the opening 'Yes'.

medium.q: Where does the comma go? 'After lunch we played cricket'.
medium.why: A comma follows an opening phrase.

medium.q: Choose the correct apostrophe: This is ___ pen.
medium.why: The apostrophe + s shows possession.

medium.q: Which is an interrogative sentence?
medium.why: It asks a question.

medium.q: Which sentence needs an exclamation mark?
medium.why: It shows excitement.

medium.q: Which sentence is declarative?
o: Is the Taj Mahal in Agra?
The Taj Mahal is in Agra.
How grand the Taj Mahal is!
medium.why: It states a fact.

hard.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Mother said, please wash your hands.
Mother said: Please, wash your hands.
hard.why: Direct speech needs a comma, quotation marks and a capital letter inside.

hard.q: Many boys left bags on the bench. Which sentence is correct?
o: The boys' bags are on the bench.
The boy's bags are on the bench.
The boys bags' are on the bench.
The boys's bags are on the bench.
hard.why: Plural boys takes only an apostrophe after the s.

hard.q: Which uses 'its' and 'it's' correctly?
o: Its raining, and the dog is in it's kennel.
It's raining, and the dog is in it's kennel.
Its raining, and the dog is in its' kennel.
It's raining, and the dog is in its kennel.
hard.why: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

hard.q: Which is the correct imperative sentence?
o: Will you pass the salt please.
hard.why: It gives a polite command.

hard.q: Which sentence has the commas right?
o: Ria my cousin, is a doctor.
Ria, my cousin, is a doctor.
Ria, my cousin is, a doctor.
Ria my, cousin is a doctor.
hard.why: Commas set off extra information.

hard.q: Which sentence is exclamatory and correctly punctuated?
hard.why: An exclamation ends with !, and 'How tall ... is' keeps the statement order.

easy.q: Choose the synonym of 'big'.
easy.why: Large means big.

easy.q: Choose the antonym of 'hot'.
easy.why: Cold is the opposite of hot.

easy.q: Choose the synonym of 'happy'.
easy.why: Glad is close in meaning to happy.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: I can ___ the bell. (hear/here)
easy.why: Hear is what ears do.

easy.q: Choose the antonym of 'early'.
easy.why: Late is the opposite of early.

easy.q: Choose the correct word: Come ___ and sit. (hear/here)
easy.why: 'Here' means in this place.

medium.q: Choose the synonym of 'begin'.
medium.why: Start means begin.

medium.q: Choose the antonym of 'ancient'.
medium.why: Modern is the opposite of ancient.

medium.q: Choose the synonym of 'brave'.
medium.why: Courageous means brave.

medium.q: Choose the right word: The ___ of the cake was delicious. (piece/peace)
medium.why: Piece means a part; peace is calm.

medium.q: Choose the antonym of 'generous'.
medium.why: Stingy means unwilling to give.

medium.q: Choose the right word: I like to ___ a book every week. (read/red)
medium.why: Read is the verb; red is a colour.

hard.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'rapid'.
hard.why: Swift means fast.

hard.q: Choose the antonym of 'victory'.
hard.why: Defeat is the opposite of victory.

hard.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'enormous'.
hard.why: Gigantic means very large.

hard.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: The principal gave a speech about good principles.
The principle gave a speech about good principals.
The principal gave a speech about good principals.
The principle gave a speech about good principles.
hard.why: Principal = head; principle = rule.

hard.q: Choose the antonym of 'expand'.
hard.why: Shrink is the opposite of expand.

hard.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Please except this gift from us.
Please accept this gift from us.
Please expect this gift from us.
Please excepting this gift from us.
hard.why: Accept means to receive; except means 'other than'.

easy.q: When water boils and turns into a gas, what is the gas called?
easy.why: Boiling water changes into water vapour, which goes into the air.

easy.q: What is the solid form of water called?
easy.why: Water becomes ice when it freezes.

easy.q: Which of these water sources is salty?
easy.why: Ocean water has salt in it. Wells, hand pumps and rain give fresh water.

easy.q: An ice cube is left in a warm room. What does it become?
easy.why: Heat melts ice into liquid water.

easy.q: Which of these is a source of fresh water?
easy.why: River water is not salty. Oceans, seas and salt lakes are salty.

easy.q: Which of these gives us groundwater?
easy.why: A well is dug down to the water that is stored under the ground.

medium.q: A glass of cold water has drops on its outside. Where did the drops come from?
o: Water leaking through tiny holes in the glass
Water that was poured on it earlier
Water vapour in the air that cooled down
medium.why: Vapour in the air cools on the cold glass and turns into drops. This is condensation.

medium.q: Why can we not drink ocean water?
o: It has no water in it
medium.why: Ocean water has a lot of salt, so it is not fit to drink.

medium.q: Water vapour rises high up and cools. It then forms tiny drops that make ...
medium.why: The drops gather in the sky as clouds.

medium.q: A puddle slowly dries up in the Sun. What happens to its water?
o: It soaks into the sky as ice
It turns into vapour and goes into the air
medium.why: The Sun heats the water and it changes into vapour.

medium.q: Which pair shows two forms of water?
medium.why: Ice is solid water and steam is water as a gas. Smoke, salt and sand are not water.

medium.q: Why does less rainwater soak into the ground in cities?
o: The soil in cities is too hot
Cement and concrete cover the ground and stop water soaking in
Rainwater is too heavy to soak in
medium.why: Roads and floors are covered with cement. The water runs off instead of going into the ground.

hard.q: A tap drips 3 litres of water every day. A school has 5 such taps. How many litres are wasted in 7 days?
hard.why: 3 x 5 = 15 litres a day, and 15 x 7 = 105 litres.

hard.q: A family uses 3 buckets of water a day for bathing and 2 for washing clothes. Each bucket holds 20 litres. How many litres do they use in 4 days?
hard.why: 5 buckets x 20 = 100 litres a day, and 100 x 4 = 400 litres.

hard.q: The Sun heats a lake and later rain falls from clouds. Which pair names the first two steps?
hard.why: Water first turns to vapour (evaporation), then the vapour cools into cloud drops (condensation).

hard.q: Which order of steps in the water cycle is correct?
o: Rain falls, clouds form, the Sun heats water, vapour rises
The Sun heats water, vapour rises, vapour cools into clouds, rain falls
Vapour cools into clouds, the Sun heats water, rain falls, vapour rises
The Sun heats water, rain falls, vapour rises, clouds form
hard.why: Heat makes vapour first. The vapour cools into clouds. Then rain falls.

hard.q: A cold plate with ice cubes in a warm room gets wet on its outside. Ravi says the ice melted and leaked out. What is the better explanation?
o: Vapour in the air cooled on the cold plate and became drops
The plate made water by itself
The room air turned into ice first
hard.why: The outside is dry before it gets cold. Drops form from vapour in the air, so no leak is needed.

hard.q: A leaking tap wastes 4 litres of water every day. How much water is wasted in 30 days?
hard.why: 4 x 30 = 120 litres. Fixing small leaks saves a lot of water.

easy.q: Where does a river usually begin?
easy.why: Many rivers start high up in the hills from springs or melting snow.

easy.q: A river starts in the hills. Where does it usually end?
easy.why: Most rivers flow down and join the sea.

easy.q: Which job depends directly on a river?
easy.why: A fisherman catches fish from the river for a living.

easy.q: A small river that joins a bigger river is called a ...
easy.why: A tributary brings its water into a bigger river.

easy.q: What is a dam built across a river used for?
easy.why: A dam holds back water so it can be used later.

easy.q: The Godavari mostly flows through which part of India?
easy.why: The Godavari flows across Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and nearby states.

medium.q: Why did people long ago build homes near rivers?
o: They could get water for drinking and farming easily
medium.why: River water gave them food, drink and water for crops.

medium.q: Which is a problem that can come after a dam is built?
o: The river turns into sand at once
People living where the reservoir fills may lose their homes
medium.why: The land behind a dam is filled with water, so homes and fields can go under.

medium.q: Which river flows through Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh?
medium.why: The Godavari flows through these states and a few more.

medium.q: Which household habit harms rivers the most?
o: Pouring strong chemical cleaners into drains that reach the river
medium.why: Chemicals flow with the drain water into rivers and harm plants and animals.

medium.q: Why are too many algae in a river bad for fish?
o: They give fish too much oxygen
When they rot they use up the oxygen in the water
They make the water warm and sweet
medium.why: Rotting algae use up oxygen, so fish may not be able to breathe.

medium.q: Why do farmers near a river often grow more crops?
o: The soil near rivers is always dry
The river gives water to water their fields
Fields near rivers get no rain
medium.why: River water can be used to irrigate fields.

hard.q: A farm takes 2,500 litres of canal water every day. How many litres does it take in 12 days?
A village pump gives 600 litres each hour and runs for 4 hours. The tank holds 3,000 litres. What is true?
o: It gives 2,400 litres and the tank is full
It gives 2,400 litres and the tank is not full
It gives 3,000 litres and the tank is full
It gives 1,800 litres and the tank is full
hard.why: 600 x 4 = 2,400 litres, which is 600 less than 3,000.

hard.q: A town upstream lets untreated waste into a river. Who is most hurt by it?
o: Only people in the town itself
Villages downstream that use the water
Only people living by the sea
hard.why: Water carries the waste downstream to everyone who uses it.

hard.q: A new dam floods a village. What is the best step?
o: Give the families new homes and land first
Close the dam and forget the village
Tell people to move without help
hard.why: People who lose their homes need new homes and land that are safe.

hard.q: What is the main trade-off of building a big dam?
o: It gives no benefit at all
It gives water and power, but some people may lose homes and land
hard.why: Dams help many people, but they can force others to move away.

hard.q: Why do fish die when a factory lets dirty water into a river?
o: The fish get too much food
The water gets poisoned and has less oxygen
hard.why: Dirty water has harmful stuff and uses up oxygen that fish need.

easy.q: Raisins are made by drying which fruit?
easy.why: Sun-drying grapes gives raisins.

easy.q: What are the tiny living things that spoil food called?
easy.why: Microbes are too small to see. They grow in food and spoil it.

easy.q: Which fruit is mostly in season in summer in much of India?
easy.why: Mangoes ripen in summer. Peas, carrots and oranges are mostly winter produce.

easy.q: Which teeth at the back grind food?
easy.why: Molars are wide and flat, so they grind food.

easy.q: Which teeth at the front are used to cut food?
easy.why: Incisors are sharp and flat. They cut food.

easy.q: Where does digestion of food begin?
easy.why: Chewing and saliva begin breaking down food in the mouth.

medium.q: Why do we dry mango slices in the Sun to make aam papad?
o: Without water, microbes cannot grow easily
medium.why: Microbes need water, so dried food stays good for longer.

medium.q: Which food will spoil fastest in a hot room?
medium.why: Wet, cooked food spoils fast. Dry rice, salt and sugar last long.

medium.q: Which is an old way to keep food from spoiling?
o: Keeping it in a warm wet place
medium.why: Dry food has no water. Microbes cannot grow without water.

medium.q: What makes idli batter fluffy?
o: Tiny microbes that make gas bubbles
medium.why: Microbes in the batter make gas, and the bubbles make it rise.

medium.q: Ghee lasts longer than butter without a fridge. Why?
o: Ghee has no water left in it, so microbes cannot grow easily
medium.why: Butter has water and milk solids, so it spoils sooner. Ghee does not.

medium.q: Why does a layer of oil help keep pickle fresh?
o: The oil keeps air away from the pickle
The oil makes the jar warm
medium.why: Microbes need air to grow. Oil blocks the air.

hard.q: 5 kg of fresh mango slices lose 3 kg of water when dried. How heavy is the dried mango?
hard.why: 5 - 3 = 2 kg is left after the water goes.

hard.q: Milk stays fresh for 2 days outside the fridge. In the fridge it lasts 4 days longer. For how many days does it last in the fridge?
hard.why: 2 + 4 = 6 days.

hard.q: Two jars have the same cut fruit. After 2 days only the jar on the shelf smells sour. What explains this?
o: The shelf made the fruit sweeter
Cold in the fridge slows down the microbes
hard.why: Microbes grow slowly in cold places.

hard.q: Which shows the way food moves in our body?
o: Mouth, stomach, food pipe, small intestine
Stomach, mouth, food pipe, small intestine
Mouth, small intestine, stomach, food pipe
Mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine
hard.why: Food is chewed in the mouth. It then goes down the food pipe to the stomach and the small intestine.

hard.q: Which food and method are matched correctly?
hard.why: Sun-drying removes water from mango slices. The other pairs use the wrong method.

hard.q: A cut fruit goes bad faster than a whole fruit. Why?
o: The cut part lets microbes in easily
hard.why: The skin protects the fruit. Cutting it opens a way for microbes.

easy.q: In many schools, the green bin is for which kind of waste?
easy.why: Green bins take wet waste such as peels and leftover food.

easy.q: Fruit peels go into which kind of waste bin?
easy.why: Peels are food waste. That is wet waste.

easy.q: Which of these goes into the blue bin for dry waste?
easy.why: Paper is dry waste. Peels, scraps and tea leaves are wet waste.

easy.q: Which is a good road rule near school?
easy.why: The footpath keeps walkers away from traffic.

easy.q: A classmate falls and gets hurt. What should you do first?
easy.why: A teacher can give help quickly.

easy.q: Whom should you tell if you face a difficulty at school?
easy.why: A teacher can help you and keep you safe.

medium.q: Why should we keep wet and dry waste in separate bins?
o: Wet waste can become compost and dry waste can be recycled
It makes the bins fill faster
medium.why: Sorted waste can be used again instead of going to a dump.

medium.q: Which of these can be recycled?
medium.why: Paper can be made into new paper. The others are wet waste for compost.

medium.q: Which of these is dry waste?
medium.why: Paper is dry waste. The others are food waste.

medium.q: Two glasses of water are kept for an hour, one under a tree and one in the Sun. Which glass is cooler?
o: The Sun one, as sunlight is cool
medium.why: Shade cuts off the Sun's heat, so the water stays cooler.

medium.q: A roof painted white stays cooler because white ...
o: takes in most of the sunlight
medium.why: Light colours throw back sunlight, so less heat enters.

medium.q: Which colour of floor tile stays cooler in the hot Sun?
medium.why: White reflects most of the Sun's heat. Dark colours take in more heat.

hard.q: A dripping tap fills a 250 mL glass in 5 minutes. How much water drips in 1 hour?
hard.why: 1 hour has 12 five-minute parts, and 12 x 250 = 3,000 mL (3 litres).

hard.q: A school makes 6 kg of wet waste and 9 kg of dry waste daily. What is the total waste in 5 days?
hard.why: 6 + 9 = 15 kg a day, and 15 x 5 = 75 kg.

hard.q: Smoke fills the corridor during a fire. What is the best action?
o: Keep low and walk out by the exit towards the assembly point
hard.why: Clean air is near the floor, and the exit leads to safety.

hard.q: The fire alarm rings at school. What should you do?
o: Walk calmly to the assembly point
hard.why: Stay calm, follow your teacher and go to the assembly point. Do not go back inside.

hard.q: Which plan best reduces waste in the school canteen?
o: Use new plastic plates every day
Use steel plates and bring own bottles
hard.why: Reusable items make less waste than throw-away ones.

hard.q: Why is collecting rainwater from the roof a good idea?
o: It saves water and helps fill the water under the ground
hard.why: Stored rainwater can be used later. Rainwater that soaks in also refills groundwater.

easy.q: Which is India's national bird?
easy.why: The peacock is the national bird of India.

easy.q: On which date do we celebrate Republic Day?
easy.why: Republic Day is on 26 January each year.

easy.q: Which colour is at the top of the Indian flag?
easy.why: The top band is saffron, then white, then green.

easy.q: Which is India's national flower?
easy.why: The lotus is our national flower.

easy.q: Which animal is India's national animal?
easy.why: The tiger is India's national animal.

easy.q: Which is India's national tree?
easy.why: The banyan is our national tree.

medium.q: What does the white band in our flag stand for?
medium.why: White shows peace and truth.

medium.q: Which animal is shown on India's national emblem?
medium.why: The emblem shows lions from the Ashoka Pillar. The tiger is the national animal.

medium.q: How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra in our flag have?
medium.why: The wheel in the middle of the flag has 24 spokes.

medium.q: Where is the Republic Day parade held every year?
medium.why: The main parade is on Kartavya Path in New Delhi.

medium.q: On Independence Day, who hoists the flag at the Red Fort?
medium.why: The Prime Minister hoists the flag and speaks to the nation from the Red Fort.

medium.q: Why do we celebrate Republic Day on 26 January?
o: The first school opened that day
India won a cricket match that day
The Constitution came into effect on that day in 1950
The Taj Mahal was built that day
medium.why: On 26 January 1950 India's Constitution began. That made India a republic.

hard.q: India became a republic in 1950. How many years is that by 2030?
Which pair is matched correctly?
hard.why: The banyan is the national tree. The national animal is the tiger, the bird the peacock and the flower the lotus.

hard.q: At a fair there are Bhangra from Punjab, Bihu from Assam and Garba from Gujarat. What does this show?
o: Dances differ by state, yet all belong to one country
hard.why: Many cultures living together as one nation is unity in diversity.

hard.q: Which sentence best explains 'unity in diversity'?
o: Everyone in India speaks the same language
People speak many languages and have many customs, yet live together as one country
hard.why: India has many languages and customs, but its people share one country.

hard.q: Which monument is shown on the Rs 50 note?
hard.why: The Rs 50 note shows the stone chariot of Hampi.

hard.q: Which pair is matched correctly?
hard.why: The banyan is India's national tree. The national flower is the lotus, the bird is the peacock and the fruit is the mango.

easy.q: Which forest in West Bengal is famous for mangroves?
easy.why: The Sundarbans is a huge mangrove forest.

easy.q: In which sea are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands?
easy.why: These islands lie in the Bay of Bengal.

easy.q: Which big cat is famous in the Sundarbans?
easy.why: The Sundarbans is home to Bengal tigers.

easy.q: Which mountain range runs along the west coast of India?
easy.why: The Western Ghats lie along the west coast.

easy.q: Which of these is a state in North-East India?
easy.why: Assam is in the North-East. The others are not.

easy.q: Which group of islands is part of India?
easy.why: Lakshadweep is a group of coral islands in the Arabian Sea.

medium.q: Why are many houses in the north-east built on bamboo stilts?
o: To stay safe from floods, damp and animals
medium.why: Heavy rain and floods are common there, so raised houses are safer.

medium.q: How do mangrove roots protect the coast?
o: They hold the soil and slow down waves
medium.why: Roots hold the mud and reduce the force of waves.

medium.q: Which of these rivers starts in the Western Ghats?
medium.why: The Kaveri starts in the Western Ghats. The others start elsewhere.

medium.q: Why were forts often built on hilltops?
o: Enemies could be seen from far and it was hard to attack
Water is easy to find there
medium.why: A high place gave a wide view and was easy to defend.

medium.q: Why are coral reefs important for sea animals?
medium.why: Many fish and sea creatures live and feed in coral reefs.

medium.q: Where do mangrove trees grow?
o: In salty, muddy water where rivers meet the sea
medium.why: Mangroves grow near the coast where river water meets sea water.

hard.q: A boat travels at 8 km per hour for 3 hours to a Sundarbans village. How far does it go?
Meena walks 6 km on each of 4 days in the Western Ghats and 5 km on the last day. How far does she walk in all?
Which shows living in harmony with nature in the north-east?
o: Making houses and bridges of bamboo and roots while keeping the forest
hard.why: Using local materials gently shows respect for nature.

hard.q: Some mangrove roots stick up out of the mud. Why?
o: They help the trees breathe in muddy soil
hard.why: Mud has little air. The upward roots take in air for the tree.

hard.q: Living root bridges in Meghalaya grow stronger over time. Why?
o: The wood becomes harder to rust
The roots of the living trees keep growing and thicken
hard.why: Living roots keep growing, so the bridge becomes stronger.

hard.q: A coastal village cuts down its mangrove forest. What is most likely to happen?
o: There is more shade on the beach
The coast faces more damage from storms and waves
hard.why: Mangrove roots hold the soil and slow down waves and storms.

easy.q: Which of these is a fuel used for cooking?
easy.why: LPG burns and gives the heat for cooking.

easy.q: What gives our body the energy to play and study?
easy.why: Food stores energy that our body uses.

easy.q: The Sun gives us which two things?
easy.why: Sunlight brings both light and heat.

easy.q: A windmill uses which kind of energy to turn?
easy.why: Moving air pushes the blades round.

easy.q: Which of these needs petrol to run?
easy.why: A scooter's engine burns petrol.

easy.q: Which of these needs electricity to work?
easy.why: A fan runs on electricity.

medium.q: Which of these will get used up one day?
medium.why: Coal is a fuel that takes millions of years to form. Wind, sunlight and water keep coming.

medium.q: Why is burning too much wood and coal a problem?
o: The smoke harms the air and our lungs
medium.why: Smoke from burning fuels pollutes the air.

medium.q: Which of these energy sources will not run out?
medium.why: The Sun keeps shining. Coal, petrol and diesel can run out.

medium.q: Water falling on a turbine in a dam helps to make ...
medium.why: Moving water turns the turbine and produces electricity.

medium.q: A solar cooker works using ...
medium.why: It collects the heat of sunlight to cook food.

medium.q: A battery in a torch stores energy. When we switch the torch on, what do we get?
medium.why: The stored energy changes into light.

hard.q: A bulb uses 0.06 units of electricity in an hour. It stays on 5 hours daily for 30 days. How many units does it use?
hard.why: 0.06 x 5 x 30 = 9 units.

hard.q: A scooter runs 45 km on 1 litre and a car runs 15 km on 1 litre. For 90 km, how many more litres does the car need?
hard.why: The scooter needs 2 litres and the car 6, so the car needs 4 more.

hard.q: Which pair of energy sources is both clean and renewable?
hard.why: Sunlight and wind do not run out and make no smoke.

hard.q: Why is solar energy better than coal for clean air?
o: Solar energy is made of coal
hard.why: Burning coal makes smoke and harmful gases. Solar energy does not.

hard.q: A village far from the power lines needs light and water pumping. Which is the best choice?
o: A diesel generator for all day use
Solar panels, as sunlight is free and clean
hard.why: Solar power needs no fuel and no smoke.

hard.q: Which action saves energy?
o: Keep all lights on in the day
Leave the TV on while you sleep
Switch off the fan and light when you leave the room
hard.why: Switching off what you are not using saves energy.

easy.q: Jute is used to make ...
easy.why: Jute fibre makes rough sacks and ropes.

easy.q: Cotton cloth comes from which source?
easy.why: Cotton fibre grows in the fruit of the cotton plant.

easy.q: Which of these is a synthetic fibre?
easy.why: Nylon is made in factories. The others are natural.

easy.q: Pashmina wool comes from the hair of which animal?
easy.why: Pashmina is the fine under-wool of mountain goats.

easy.q: Wool for sweaters mostly comes from which animal?
easy.why: Sheep hair is cut, spun into yarn and used to make wool.

easy.q: What does a tailor use to join pieces of cloth?
easy.why: Stitching joins cloth with thread.

medium.q: Which tool is used to weave cloth?
medium.why: A loom holds the threads while cloth is woven.

medium.q: What is spinning?
medium.why: Spinning twists loose fibres into a strong thread.

medium.q: Silk threads come from the cocoon of which insect?
medium.why: The silkworm spins a cocoon of silk thread.

medium.q: How are threads joined in weaving?
o: By crossing them over and under each other
medium.why: Weaving crosses threads at right angles.

medium.q: Why do we wear woollen clothes in winter?
o: Wool traps warm air close to the body
medium.why: Trapped warm air keeps us warm.

medium.q: What happens in weaving?
o: Threads are tied in one long knot
Threads cross over and under each other
medium.why: In weaving, one set of threads goes over and under another set.

hard.q: A tailor makes 5 shirts a day using 2 m of cloth each. How much cloth is used in 6 days?
hard.why: 5 x 2 = 10 m a day, and 10 x 6 = 60 m.

hard.q: One silk saree needs 6 m of silk cloth. A shop has 54 m. How many sarees can be made?
hard.why: 54 divided by 6 is 9.

hard.q: Which stage of the silk moth comes just before the cocoon?
hard.why: The caterpillar spins the cocoon around itself.

hard.q: Which order shows the life cycle of the silk moth?
hard.why: The moth lays eggs. A caterpillar hatches, spins a cocoon, and a moth comes out.

hard.q: Why can synthetic cloth feel uncomfortable in summer?
o: It is too thin to see
hard.why: Cotton absorbs sweat, but synthetic cloth often does not.

hard.q: Why are cotton clothes comfortable in hot weather?
o: Cotton soaks up sweat and lets air pass
Cotton keeps all the air out
hard.why: Cotton takes in sweat and lets air move, so we stay cooler.

easy.q: Which season is the hottest in most of India?
easy.why: Summer has the highest heat.

easy.q: What causes day and night?
o: The Sun goes round the Earth
The Earth spins on its axis
easy.why: The Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day and the other side has night.

easy.q: Which season follows summer in most of India?
easy.why: Rains come after the hot summer.

easy.q: The Earth turns once around itself in about ...
easy.why: One turn gives one day and night.

easy.q: In which season does most of India get heavy rain?
easy.why: The monsoon brings heavy rain to most of India.

easy.q: The side of the Earth facing the Sun has ...
easy.why: The Sun lights that side, so it has day.

medium.q: In which season do many trees get new leaves and flowers?
medium.why: New leaves and blossoms appear in spring.

medium.q: Why is Kashmir colder in winter than Kerala?
o: It is far north and high in the mountains
medium.why: Kashmir lies far north and high, so it is cold.

medium.q: When it is day in India, it is night in which country?
medium.why: The USA is on almost the opposite side of the Earth. Nepal, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are close to India.

medium.q: If the Earth stopped spinning, what would happen?
o: One side would have day for ever and the other night
medium.why: The side facing the Sun would stay lit.

medium.q: Which crop is grown mainly in the rainy season?
medium.why: Rice is a rainy season crop. Wheat is a winter crop.

medium.q: Which of these changes happens again and again every year?
medium.why: Seasons come back in the same order each year. The others happen in a day.

hard.q: A plant is 5 cm tall and grows 2 cm each week. How tall is it after 9 weeks?
In a town daylight lasts 13 hours. How many hours of night are there in that day?
Chennai stays warm all year while Delhi has hot summers and cold winters. What helps explain this?
o: The sea near Chennai keeps its temperature steady
hard.why: Land near the sea warms and cools slowly.

hard.q: Assam gets heavy monsoon rain and Rajasthan stays mostly dry. Why?
o: Assam is nearer to the Sun
Places in India have different climates and rainfall
The monsoon only visits Assam by chance
hard.why: Climate and rainfall change from place to place in India.

hard.q: Which list goes from fastest to slowest change?
o: Bubble bursting, fruit ripening, child growing, mountain wearing away
Mountain wearing away, child growing, fruit ripening, bubble bursting
Child growing, bubble bursting, mountain wearing, fruit ripening
Fruit ripening, mountain wearing, bubble bursting, child growing
hard.why: A bubble pops in a second, a fruit ripens in days, a child grows over years, and a mountain wears away over thousands of years.

hard.q: Which of these changes takes the longest time?
o: A seed growing into a big tree
The sky turning orange at sunset
hard.why: A tree takes many years. The others take minutes or hours.

easy.q: Which is the biggest ocean on Earth?
easy.why: The Pacific is the largest ocean.

easy.q: The oceans of the Earth are ...
easy.why: Water flows from one ocean to the next. They form one big ocean.

easy.q: Which ocean is named after our country?
easy.why: The Indian Ocean has India's name.

easy.q: A globe is a model of ...
easy.why: A globe shows the Earth's shape.

easy.q: What does 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' mean?
o: The whole world is one family
easy.why: It teaches us that all people and living things are like one family.

easy.q: Which spice reached India from South America?
easy.why: Chillies came from South America. Black pepper grew in India.

medium.q: Which food came to India from outside?
medium.why: The potato came from South America. The others grew in India.

medium.q: Chillies first came to India from which place?
medium.why: Chillies travelled from South America.

medium.q: Which of these can cross country borders freely?
medium.why: Clouds float across borders. The other things stay in one place.

medium.q: Yoga began in India and is practised across the world. What does this show?
o: Only one country can use it
medium.why: People share ideas and customs with one another.

medium.q: Smoke from a factory in one country reaches another country. What does this show?
medium.why: Wind carries smoke across countries.

medium.q: Why do some birds, like the rosy starling, come to India in winter?
o: To find food and a warmer place
medium.why: In their home it is too cold and food is hard to find, so they travel to warmer places.

hard.q: A bird flies 600 km a day for 7 days. How far does it fly in all?
A bird arrives in India on 1 November and leaves on 1 March. How many months does it stay?
hard.why: From November to March is 4 months.

hard.q: A sea turtle born on an Odisha beach swims to Australia and back. What does this show?
o: Animals do not follow country borders
Odisha is not near the sea
hard.why: Animals travel freely across countries and oceans.

hard.q: Which sentence shows that nature has no boundaries?
o: A river can flow through many countries
Every country has its own sky
hard.why: A river does not stop at borders.

hard.q: Which statement is correct?
o: Chilli began in India and pepper came from South America
Black pepper began in India and chilli came from South America
hard.why: Pepper grew in the Western Ghats, but chillies came to India from South America.

hard.q: Plastic thrown into a river in one town reaches the sea and harms animals far away. What does this show?
o: Rubbish stays where it is thrown
hard.why: Rivers carry things to the sea. What we do in one place can affect others far away.
